analysis.one_liner: Voids EPA rules limiting toxic air pollution from industrial boilers and incinerators, replacing them with weaker standards and later deadlines.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 275-142, with 41 of 192 Democrats joining all 234 voting Republicans, but the Senate never voted, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill threw out four EPA rules issued in March 2011 that limited hazardous air pollution — mercury, dioxin, particulates — from industrial, commercial, and institutional boilers, process heaters, and solid waste incinerators. It required EPA to write new rules within 15 months, barred compliance deadlines sooner than five years after those rules took effect, and directed EPA to adopt narrower waste definitions and the 'least burdensome' regulatory option. Backers said the original rules were unachievable and would close plants; opponents said the bill would prolong pollution exposure near thousands of facilities, including incinerators close to nursing homes and hospitals.
analysis.who_benefits: Operators of industrial and commercial boilers and incinerators — factories, pulp and paper mills, chemical plants, power and industrial facilities — avoid compliance costs and gain years of delay before installing pollution controls. Facilities that might have been reclassified as 'solid waste incinerators' under stricter definitions escape tighter emission limits.

how_it_helps.text: Voids four EPA rules that limited hazardous air pollutants from industrial boilers, process heaters, and solid waste incinerators, treating them 'as though they had never taken effect.'

Bars EPA from setting compliance deadlines earlier than five years after replacement rules take effect, and requires EPA to weigh compliance costs, equipment availability, and net employment impacts when setting those dates.
Directs EPA to use narrower definitions of 'commercial and industrial waste' and to identify fewer materials as solid waste, which keeps more units out of the stricter incinerator emission standards.
Requires EPA to set emission standards that sources can consistently meet under actual operating conditions and to impose the least burdensome regulatory alternative.

analysis.who_pays: People who live and work near industrial boilers and incinerators, especially communities near facilities within range of schools, nursing homes, and hospitals, would breathe more mercury, dioxin, and fine particulate pollution for at least five extra years while weaker standards are written and phased in.

drawbacks.text: The House defeated a motion to recommit that would have required EPA not to delay pollution reductions for incinerators within five miles of a nursing home, assisted living facility, or hospital, and would have required facilities facing delayed regulation to notify affected communities within 90 days — a signal that the bill offered no such protections.

Supporters acknowledged real concerns with the 2011 rules: many contended the maximum achievable control technology standards were not achievable under actual operating conditions, which is why the bill requires standards that can be met 'consistently and concurrently' in practice.

EPA still had to write replacement rules, so the bill was not full repeal; but its rigid 15-month deadline, mandatory five-year compliance delay, and 'least burdensome' mandate would have left weaker protections on the books for years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it had become law, the cost would fall on air quality and public health near thousands of industrial sites for years, while the savings went to a specific set of facilities avoiding pollution-control spending. The argument for the bill was process, not health: that the 2011 rules were technically impossible to meet. The bill responded with delay rather than a targeted fix, and it died in the Senate, so those tradeoffs were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 275-142 on October 13, 2011, and it was placed on the Senate calendar two days later, but the Senate never brought it to a vote, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The House Energy and Commerce Committee reported the bill on September 26, 2011, after approving it 36-14 in markup.

On October 13, 2011, the House rejected a Democratic motion to recommit that would have protected nursing homes and hospitals near waste incinerators from delayed pollution reductions, 170-246; 169 of 192 Democrats voted for it and 233 of 241 Republicans voted against it.
The House then passed the bill 275-142; every voting Republican (234 of 241) voted yes, joined by 41 of 192 Democrats, while 142 Democrats voted no.

The Senate received the bill on October 17, 2011, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders, where it stayed without action until the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA's 2011 boiler and incinerator rules stood, though EPA itself revised and relaxed them in later rulemaking; operators of industrial boilers and incinerators were better off than they would have been under the bill, and communities near those facilities avoided the bill's added years of delayed emission controls. Senate inaction — not House action — decided the outcome.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was 234-0 among voting Republicans; 41 of 192 Democrats joined them while 142 voted no. The motion to recommit split almost exactly on party lines (169-13 among Democrats, 1-233 among Republicans).

industries.industry: Industrial and commercial boiler and incinerator operators
industries.note: The bill voided rules requiring them to install controls for mercury, dioxin, and particulate pollution and pushed compliance at least five years out, saving them equipment and operating costs. Those savings come directly at the expense of air quality for people living and working near the facilities.

Firms that would have supplied scrubbers, filters, and monitoring equipment to thousands of facilities lost the near-term market the 2011 rules would have created. Their interest in the bill ran alongside faster cleanup.

industries.industry: Waste and biomass fuel users seeking narrower 'solid waste' definitions
industries.note: The bill ordered EPA to adopt older, narrower definitions of commercial and industrial waste, keeping more combustion units out of the stricter incinerator standards. That benefits facilities burning secondary materials, at the public's expense in unregulated emissions.
